 Part A · Q(a) 5 marks

 Explain the steps involved in the Operations Research approach to solving a problem. Why is model formulation considered a
 crucial phase?

The OR approach is a scientific, systematic, team-based method for turning a messy real-life decision problem into a quantitative
model whose solution can be implemented. It moves through six phases (the cycle is iterative — if validation fails you go back to an
earlier phase).

 # Phase What is done

 1 Problem definition Identify the decision-maker, objectives, alternative courses of action, constraints/limitations and the scope of
 (orientation) the system. A wrongly defined problem gives a perfect answer to the wrong question.

 2 Data collection & Gather the facts the model needs — costs, times, capacities, demands, probabilities — from records, surveys
 observation or measurement.

 3 Model formulation Translate the problem into a mathematical model: decision variables, an objective function (Max profit / Min
 cost) and constraints (equations/inequalities). Choose the model type (LP, transportation, assignment,
 network, game, simulation …).

 4 Solution of the model Apply a suitable technique — simplex, MODI, Hungarian, CPM, Johnson, simulation etc. — to get the optimal
 (or best feasible) solution, usually with a computer.

 5 Validation & Test whether the model predicts reality (compare with past data), check that results are sensible, and study
 sensitivity analysis how the answer changes if the data change (what-if / shadow prices).

 6 Implementation & Put the solution to work, train people, monitor results and update the model when conditions change.
 control


Why model formulation is the crucial phase
 It is the bridge between reality and mathematics: it converts vague statements (“use resources well”) into precise variables,
 objective and constraints that can be solved.
 Every later phase depends on it — an incorrect or incomplete model (missing constraint, wrong objective, wrong coefficient)
 gives a mathematically correct but useless/harmful solution: “garbage in, garbage out”.

 It decides the solution technique and the data that must be collected, so it fixes the cost and time of the whole study.
 It forces the analyst to decide what is relevant (simplification, assumptions such as linearity, certainty, divisibility) — a model
 must be simple enough to solve yet close enough to reality to be trusted.

 A good model allows cheap experimentation, what-if and sensitivity analysis instead of costly trials on the real system.

Part A · Q(d) 5 marks

 Using the concept of random number generation, demonstrate how you would simulate daily demand for a certain item in a
 shop. Explain the steps involved.

Idea (Monte-Carlo simulation): daily demand is uncertain but follows a known frequency pattern. We convert that pattern into
ranges of random numbers, then draw random numbers to “play” many days on paper/computer and study the average demand.

 1. Collect data – record past daily demand and how often each value occurred (frequency).

 2. Probability distribution – probability = frequency ÷ total days.

 3. Cumulative probability – add the probabilities one after another (last value = 1.00).

 4. Assign random-number intervals – for 2-digit random numbers (00–99), give each demand a block of numbers whose size = its
 probability (e.g. P = 0.25 ⇒ 25 numbers).

 5. Generate random numbers – from a random-number table, a calculator/Excel RAND, or a congruential generator
 Xn+1 = (a·Xn + c) mod m .

 6. Map each random number to a demand by finding which interval it falls in; this is that day's simulated demand.

 7. Repeat for N days (the larger N, the closer to reality) and compute the average / total demand, stock-outs etc.; use the result
 for decisions such as reorder level.

Factors to consider before crashing

 Crashing = shortening the project duration by spending extra money (overtime, more labour/equipment, outsourcing) on
 selected activities. Cost of crashing is the cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) ÷ (normal time − crash time).


 Only critical activities — shortening a non-critical activity does not shorten the project. Here there are two parallel critical
 paths, so the duration falls only if both paths are shortened (crash a common activity A, B or G, or one activity on each path,
 e.g. C and D).

 Cost slope — crash first the activity with the lowest cost per day saved; stop when the extra cost of one more day exceeds the
 benefit.
 Crash limit — each activity can be cut only up to its minimum feasible (crash) time; beyond that no reduction is possible.

 New critical paths — after crashing, a near-critical path (small float) can become critical; re-run the forward/backward pass
 after every step.
 Indirect costs & penalties — compare crash cost with overhead saved per day, contract penalties for delay, and incentives for
 early delivery to find the least-total-cost duration.
 Resources & feasibility — availability of extra staff, machines, editors/printers, budget; whether the task can really be
 accelerated (a technical review needs time).

 Quality, risk and safety — overtime and parallel work raise error and rework risk; precedence logic must still hold (G needs

 Stakeholders — deadline importance, customer agreement, morale and fatigue of the team.

 (RHS), all else unchanged: yi = ∂Z*/∂bi. It is the maximum price the company should be willing to pay for one more unit.

Quick Revision Sheet — Methods & Formulas

 Topic Key points to remember

 Simplex (max) Standard form: add slack for ≤ ; surplus + artificial for ≥ ; artificial for =. Enter largest positive
 Cj−Zj; leave min positive ratio XB/a. Stop when all Cj−Zj ≤ 0. Min problem: maximise −Z.

 Big-M Artificial variables get −M (max problem); M terms dominate Cj−Zj. Any artificial left in the basis
 at a positive level ⇒ infeasible.

 Dual rules Max (≤) ↔ Min (≥): RHS ↔ objective coefficients; columns ↔ rows; variables y ≥ 0; an
 equality ⇒ unrestricted dual variable. Primal 3 variables, 2 constraints ⇒ dual graphical. Strong
 duality: Z* = W*.

 Shadow price yi = ∂Z*/∂bi within the RHS range; ΔZ ≈ y·Δb; buy more if y > extra cost; zero for slack resources.

 Gomory cut Take row of a fractional XB (largest fraction): Σ fjxj ≥ f₀ with f = x − ⌊x⌋ (negatives: −2/3 → 1/3) ⇒
 −Σ fjxj + G = −f₀; dual simplex (leave most negative XB, enter min |(Cj−Zj)/a|).

 Branch & bound Solve LP relaxation; branch on fractional x (x ≤ ⌊x⌋, x ≥ ⌈x⌉); fathom if infeasible, integer, or
 bound no better than incumbent; best integer node is optimal.

 Graphical Only 2 variables; check all corner points of the feasible region; iso-profit/iso-cost line touches
 the last/first corner.

 Transportation Balance first (dummy row/col, cost 0). Need m+n−1 basic cells (else add ε). NWC top-left; LCM
 cheapest cell; VAM largest penalty = difference of two smallest costs. MODI: ui+vj = cij on basic
 cells; Δ = cij−ui−vj ≥ 0 ⇒ optimal.

 Assignment Hungarian: row min → column min → cover zeros with min lines; lines = n ⇒ assign; else
 subtract min uncovered, add at intersections. Unbalanced ⇒ dummy (0); forbidden ⇒ ∞;
 maximise ⇒ subtract from largest.

 CPM Forward pass ES/EF = ES + t; backward pass LF/LS = LF − t. Total float = LS − ES; free float =
 E(head) − EF. Critical activities: float 0. Dummy activity = zero duration, shows dependence.

 PERT te = (a+4m+b)/6; σ² = ((b−a)/6)²; project mean = Σte on critical path; σ²proj = Σσ² on it; Z = (T −
 μ)/σ.

 Crashing Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost)/(normal − crash time); crash critical activities with lowest
 slope; watch parallel critical paths; total cost = direct + indirect (U-shape).

 Game theory Row minima → maximin; column maxima → minimax; equal ⇒ saddle point (pure). Else
 dominance, then 2×2: D = a₁₁+a₂₂−a₁₂−a₂₁; p₁ = (a₂₂−a₂₁)/D; q₁ = (a₂₂−a₁₂)/D; V = (a₁₁a₂₂−a₁₂a₂₁)/D.

 Johnson (2 machines) Smallest time on M1 ⇒ first; on M2 ⇒ last. M2 start = max(M1 end, M2 previous end). Idle M1
 = total − ΣM1 (after last job); idle M2 = total − ΣM2.

 Simulation Probabilities → cumulative → random-number intervals (00–99); generate random numbers
 (table / LCG Xn+1 = (aXn+c) mod m); map to values; repeat N trials; average.

 OR phases Define problem → collect data → formulate model → solve → validate/sensitivity → implement
 & control.
